Silver is roughly halfway between copper and lead in terms of density. Copper and lead are two other metals commonly used in bullets. Until the recent usage of very precise machining, all copper bullets were generally found to be lacking in performance. Although copper bullets are hard enough to be driven at high velocities without fouling the barrel, they have low sectional density which can adversely affect their penetration. Copper bullets also wear down the rifling of a barrel more quickly. All lead bullets by contrast maximize the lifespan of barrels, have higher sectional density, but can not be driven as fast without fouling the barrel. Generally the only way to drive a lead bullet at high velocities without fouling the barrel is to encase the lead in a copper jacket.

All silver bullets could be a healthy compromise between copper and lead. Silver could be hardened enough for high velocities but have better sectional density than copper.
